title: The formation of Fe2Mo and its effects on deformation behaviors of ferrite-martensite dual-phase stainless steel
abstract: The strength and ductility of dual-phase stainless steels are strongly dependent on microstructure and the phase properties. The excessive hardness difference between the two phases leads to interface decohesion, thereby preventing the full utilization of the superior work hardening capability of the dual-phase structure. In this study, a ferrite-martensite stainless steel was developed through inducing high-density dislocations in the ferrite and regulating nanoprecipitate behavior, which in turn reduces the hardness difference between the two phases. An ultrahigh tensile strength of 2376 MPa was obtained together with a total elongation of 7.1 %. High-density dislocations were introduced into ferrite through cold rolling, followed by aging treatment that promoted the formation of three types of nanoprecipitates: Fe2Mo, Cr-rich, and Ni3Nb phases. The Cr-rich and Ni3Nb phases were uniformly distributed in both ferrite and martensite, and not affected by cold deformation. In contrast, the formation of Fe2Mo exhibited a strong dependence on deformation. Without cold rolling, Fe2Mo was distributed only within the martensite, and its volume fraction was rather low in the ferrite. The high-density dislocations provided sufficient heterogeneous nucleation sites, promoting to the formation of large amount of fine Fe2Mo within ferrite. The fine Fe2Mo particles enhanced the ferrite hardness and decreased the hardness difference between ferrite and martensite. Thus, the strengthened ferrite can deform synergistically with martensite, alleviating the strain localization and providing excellent work-hardening capability through heterogeneous deformation-induced stress.
